Wallace's essay, with its dateline and the manner of its sending, was consistent with Lyell and Hooker's statement that the two men had worked unknown to one another, and it was Wallace himself who had sent the essay to Darwin, with the express wish that Darwin forward it to Lyell if he thought it sufficiently novel and interesting.

The price is that it leaves no record of who did what.

W2-LINN.title: Darwin and Wallace, 'On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties…', Journal of the Proceedings of the Linnean Society (1858), with the covering letter of Lyell and Hooker, Wikisource
W2-LINN.ref: en:On the tendency of species to form varieties; and on the Perpetuation of Varieties and Species by Natural Means of Selection

W2-PSM.title: 'Sketch of Alfred Russel Wallace', Popular Science Monthly, vol. 11 (June 1877), Wikisource
W2-PSM.ref: en:Popular Science Monthly/Volume 11/June 1877/Sketch of Alfred Russel Wallace

episode.outcome: The source closes with the three papers read to the Linnean Society on 1 July 1858. Darwin had given Lyell and Hooker permission to use his memoir as they saw fit, and they explained to him that the arrangement served the interests of science generally, not only the question of priority.
episode.quote: On representing this to Mr. Darwin, he gave us permission to make what use we thought proper of his memoir, &c.; and in adopting our present course, of presenting it to the Linnean Society, we have explained to him that we are not solely considering the relative claims to priority of himself and his friend, but the interests of science generally

episode.outcome: The sketch records that Wallace's paper reached the Society through Lyell and was read on 1 July 1858 alongside Darwin's. It then records Wallace's later disagreement with Darwin on whether natural selection alone could explain human origins, his return to England, his medals and his publications.
episode.quote: was read before that body on July 1, 1858, coincidently with the reading of Mr, Darwin's paper

additions.why: The letter says the three items are listed by date. It does not say this was the order of reading. Readers need this to understand the scope of the A1/A2 claim that the reading order is not recorded.

claims.scope: Full text of W2-LINN and W2-PSM. Neither records a reply from Wallace or any notice to him about the reading. However, the letter says both authors 'unreservedly placed their papers in our hands'. It also says Darwin only 'proposed' to obtain Wallace's consent to publication, and was not consulted about the reading.

Add a qualification: Lyell and Hooker say both authors had 'unreservedly' placed their papers in their hands, and Darwin had proposed to seek Wallace's consent to publication. Neither source records whether Wallace knew of or agreed to the reading.

claims.scope: Full text of the Lyell–Hooker letter. The letter mentions that Darwin was urged to publish and that the world was awaiting his complete work. It does not present either point as an option that was considered.

quote.quote: while the scientific world is waiting for the appearance of Mr. Darwin's complete work

claims.fix: Keep the claim.

context_issues.problem: The title given in the sketch differs from the actual heading in the Linnean journal. The draft says '小传给出的标题', which is accurate, but it does not give the journal's own title, so readers may take the sketch's version as the original.

quote.quote: On the Tendency of Species to form Varieties; and on the Perpetuation of Varieties and Species by Natural Means of Selection.

context_issues.problem: The sketch says Wallace's paper was 'transmitted through Sir Charles Lyell'. The Linnean letter says Wallace sent the essay to Darwin, who was to forward it to Lyell. The draft quotes the sketch without noting this difference in the route of transmission.

quote.quote: for the perusal of his friend and correspondent Mr. Darwin, and sent to him with the expressed wish that it should be forwarded to Sir Charles Lyell

context_issues.problem: The draft says only that 'the evidence does not say'. It leaves out the letter's claim that both authors handed over their papers 'unreservedly'. Readers lose a source statement that bears on the question of consent.

quote.quote: both authors having now unreservedly placed their papers in our hands

review.overall: Both sources were read in full. The draft's account of how events ended matches the sources, and the claims that something is not recorded are broadly sound. Two fixes are recommended: change 'the evidence pack does not say' to 'neither source records', and add that the letter says both authors handed over their papers 'unreservedly'.
